title: The ray of light (Kern ch. 1)
hookLine: a ray from the Buddha's brow lights up countless worlds; Manjushri says a great teaching is coming
last: THE LOTUS OF THE TRUE LAW.

cards: In a theater, a moment before the play, the house lights go down. Programs stop rustling. Phones go dark.
Nobody has said a word, but everyone knows something is about to start. The Lotus Sutra opens with a moment like that, only the stage is a mountain and the light comes from the Buddha himself.
He has just finished teaching. He goes silent, sits in deep meditation, and then something happens that nobody in the crowd can explain.

teach.b: The Buddha is on the Vulture Peak, a mountain near the city of Rajagriha, with a vast crowd: monks and nuns, bodhisattvas, kings, gods and spirits. He finishes a teaching, sits cross-legged and goes into deep meditation.
Flowers rain down from the sky. The ground trembles. Everyone falls silent and looks at him.
From the tuft of white hair between his eyebrows, a single ray of light goes out toward the east, and in Kern's telling it lights up worlds upon worlds.
In its light the crowd sees everything at once: beings in every kind of life, Buddhas teaching, bodhisattvas practicing, monuments to Buddhas long gone.
The bodhisattva Maitreya wonders what this means, and so does everyone else.
So he asks Manjushri, the bodhisattva of wisdom, who answers from memory. Long ago, a Buddha named Moon-Sun-Lamp did exactly this: the meditation, the flowers, the ray.
And when he rose, he taught the Lotus of the True Law. So the same is about to happen now. A great teaching is coming.
Then the twist. In that old story, Manjushri says, he himself was a bodhisattva named Varaprabha. And there was a disciple called Fame-Seeker, who loved gain and kept forgetting what he learned.
Who was that? It was you, Maitreya.
The one asking the question was once the slow student.
The ray lights up worlds upon worlds, and it lands, gently, on him.

how: Mahayana Buddhists who chant and study the Lotus Sutra begin with its opening scene on Vulture Peak, where the ray of light sets up everything that follows.

games.q: what does “the ray of light” mean?
o: the first sunrise the Buddha saw after waking up
the light from the Buddha's brow that opens the Lotus
the glow of the sunset over the Vulture Peak

games.q: a great teaching comes: tap the pairs.
p: the mountain where the sutra opens
from the hair between the Buddha's brows
remembers a Buddha who did the same

s: Manjushri says he has no idea what the light means
he remembers a past Buddha who did the same, then taught the Lotus; so a great teaching is coming.
the ray comes from between the Buddha's eyebrows
from the tuft of white hair there, shining out toward the east.
Fame-Seeker, the forgetful disciple, was Manjushri
Manjushri was Varaprabha; Fame-Seeker was Maitreya, the one asking.

games.q: Manjushri tells of a forgetful disciple long ago called Fame-Seeker, who loved gain. who does he say that disciple was?
o: Maitreya, the one asking the question
games.why: it was Maitreya. the bodhisattva asking what the light means was once the slow student in the old story.

practice: Find where the light is in the room, a window, a lamp, a shine on a glass, and let your eyes rest there. Notice how it shows you things you weren't looking at a minute ago: a corner, the grain of a table.
If your eyes are closed, notice the faint light that still comes through the lids, and wait quietly, the way the crowd waited on the mountain.

wordCard.voice: The ray of light. In the Lotus Sutra's first chapter, a ray from the Buddha's brow lights up worlds to the east, and Manjushri says a great teaching is on its way. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Manjushri, the bodhisattva of wisdom, who explains the ray of light in the Lotus Sutra's first chapter.

carryVoice: Your line: a great teaching comes. Even the slow student was in the light. See you tomorrow.
